name: Digital Signature
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: The Signature That Cannot Be Copied
lesson.summary: A digital signature uses a private key to produce a value that anyone holding the matching public key can verify, proving both who approved a message and that the message was not altered.
lesson.body:
A handwritten signature is a strange piece of security theater. It never changes no matter what document it sits on, which means anyone who has seen it once can trace or paste it onto a different page. It proves almost nothing about the content it is attached to. Digital signatures were designed to fix exactly this weakness. Instead of a fixed mark, a digital signature is a value computed from both the signer's private key and the specific content being signed, so the signature itself changes every time the message changes, even by one character.

The mechanics build directly on key pair generation. A signer does not usually run their entire message through the signing algorithm. Messages can be gigabytes long, and signing algorithms like RSA or ECDSA are built to operate efficiently on fixed-size inputs, so in practice the signer first computes a hash of the message and signs that fixed-size digest with their private key. The result, the signature, is then sent along with the original message. A verifier recomputes the hash of the received message and uses the signer's public key to check that the signature matches. If either the message or the signature has been altered in transit, the check fails.

This one mechanism delivers two separate guarantees at once. The first is authenticity: only someone in possession of the private key could have produced a signature that verifies correctly against the corresponding public key, assuming the underlying math (factoring large numbers for RSA, or the discrete logarithm problem on an elliptic curve for ECDSA) remains computationally hard to break. The second is integrity: because the signature covers a hash of the exact message, changing even a single bit of the message after signing produces a completely different hash, and the old signature no longer verifies against it. Tampering is not just detectable, it is what breaks the whole check.

Bitcoin gives a concrete, everyday example of this at work. When Alice wants to spend coins from her address, she constructs a transaction and signs it with the private key associated with that address, using the ECDSA scheme over the secp256k1 curve. Every node that receives the transaction independently verifies the signature against Alice's public key before accepting it into a block. No central authority checks Alice's identity in the moment; the math of the signature does the checking. If someone intercepts and edits the transaction, perhaps changing the payment amount, the signature no longer matches and every honest node rejects it.

It is worth being precise about what a signature is not. Signing a message does not hide it. Encryption and signing solve different problems: encryption uses a key to make content unreadable to anyone without the corresponding decryption key, while signing leaves the content fully visible and instead attaches proof of origin and integrity. Some protocols do both, encrypting a message and then signing the ciphertext, but they are separate steps solving separate problems, and confusing them is a common and consequential mistake.
